set1.q: What does nevus flammeus look like early in life, and later?
opts: Early, a bright red papule or plaque that grows rapidly; later, a pale involuted patch with residual telangiectasia
That is the infantile hemangioma's course.
Early, small pink macules on the nape of the neck; later, complete fading within the first year
That is nevus simplex.
Early, a smooth firm deep red papule under five millimetres; later, more of the same on the trunk
That is the cherry angioma.
Early, a flat blanchable patch; later, a raised thickened plaque of deeper colour

Correct — early it is well-circumscribed and macular, pink to red to purple, usually unilateral with fairly sharp midline cutoffs, and it darkens with crying, fever or overheating. Later the vasculature dilates and it may become a raised, thickened, deep-red to purple plaque.

Intertriginous freckling; the freckles are under five millimetres

Axillary freckling over fifteen millimetres, larger than a café au lait spot, present from birth
The freckles are smaller than café au lait spots, not larger.
A dimple appearing on lateral compression of a firm dermal nodule
That is the dimple sign of dermatofibroma.

The cone-shaped central keratin core, because it is what transmits the pressure down into the skin

The proliferating endothelial cells, because they are what drive the lesion to keep enlarging over months

Necrotic tissue, eschar and slough, because they promote infection, delay granulation and impede healing

A wound care specialist, and surgery for debridement or wound closure

Mechanical trauma such as ill-fitting shoes, causing hyperkeratosis with a cone-shaped central core of hard keratin pointing into the skin

Broad-area friction such as manual work, causing diffuse hyperkeratosis with no central core and a poorly defined margin

It is benign and often resolves over months to years; treatment is available if wanted

opts: Proliferation of endothelial cells from a gene mutation, present in the first weeks of life
That is the infantile hemangioma.
Dilation of dermal capillaries present from birth, darkening and thickening throughout life
That is nevus flammeus.
Dilation of preexisting vessels in estrogen excess; no proliferation

Proliferation of new capillaries and venules with age, with no hormonal association at all

Correct — pink to erythematous blanchable macules or patches, single or multiple.

Face and upper trunk; pregnancy

opts: Persistent non-blanchable deep red or purple discolouration; the skin can be intact or non-intact
Correct — the colour is the finding, and intact skin does not exclude it.
Obscured full thickness loss whose extent cannot be determined because of slough or eschar
That is unstageable.
A localised area of non-blanchable erythema of intact skin, without discolouration in depth
That is stage 1, where the change is superficial erythema.
Full thickness skin and tissue loss exposing fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, cartilage or bone

Correct — a hair may occasionally be seen protruding from a sinus opening.
Acutely, recurrent purulent drainage from several sinus tracts; chronically, sudden pain and swelling over the sacrum
This reverses the acute and chronic presentations.
Acutely, a rapidly growing vascular nodule that bleeds easily; chronically, a flat uniformly pigmented patch
That describes pyogenic granuloma and a lentigo instead.
Acutely, non-blanchable erythema over intact skin; chronically, a deep ulcer extending as far as bone
That is the pressure injury staging spectrum.

Reduces recurrence by removing the entire cyst capsule

Reduces scar erythema by reducing neovascularization

Reduces scar height by cross-linking collagen fibers

opts: It comes from repeated scratching, is lichenified with exaggerated skin markings, is plaque-like, and itches intensely

It comes from broad-area pressure, is diffusely thickened without a central core, is larger and irregular, and is usually painless

It comes from focal pressure, has a cone-shaped keratin core, is smaller and well defined, and hurts on direct pressure

That is the dermatofibroma.
Firm bulbous nodules or elevated plaques extending beyond a wound; pruritic or burning if symptomatic
That is the keloid.
Soft pedunculated papules on a narrow stalk, one to ten millimetres; symptomatic only if torn
That is the acrochordon.
Soft painless subcutaneous nodules, rubbery, usually under five centimetres
Correct — asymptomatic unless adjoining structures are invaded, and it can occur anywhere on the body.

opts: Intralesional corticosteroid alone, with fluorouracil added if the lesion continues to enlarge
Fluorouracil is a keloid treatment in this lecture.
Surgical excision in every case, performed before the proliferative phase has finished

Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen, repeated until the lesion has flattened completely
Cryotherapy is not offered for these lesions.
Beta-blockers and corticosteroids; both are named first line

Increased in males two to one, on the face, the scalp, the neck and the trunk; very common and occurring at any adult age

Increased in females two to one, on the legs and the arms, and found in all races; a common lesion appearing after minor trauma

Hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, remodeling

Inflammation, hemostasis, remodeling, proliferation

Only in immunosuppressed patients, in whom the lesion behaves more aggressively

set1.q: What does the deck call the best measure against pressure injury, and what does it include?
opts: Occlusive dressings: silicone gel sheeting worn twelve to twenty-four hours a day over every bony prominence at risk
Silicone sheeting is a scar treatment in this lecture.
Prevention: frequent skin assessment, nutrition assessment, moisture control and skin care, repositioning every two hours, pain management, improved mobility and specialty mattresses
Correct — barrier creams and incontinence management sit under moisture control.
Early debridement: removal of the necrotic tissue, eschar and slough that promote infection, delay granulation and impede healing, as soon as any injury is identified at any stage

Prophylactic antibiotics: routinely covering skin flora in every immobile patient in order to prevent any wound infection before it has a chance to start

Punch biopsy of the cyst wall before any excision

Usually none
Correct — the diagnosis is clinical.
Culture of the expressed material in every case
Culture is not part of the routine diagnosis.

opts: Obesity, repeated local trauma or irritation, a sedentary lifestyle, increased hair density in the natal cleft, and a positive family history for the same lesion in a first-degree relative
Those are the pilonidal cyst risk factors.
African American, Hispanic or Asian ancestry, together with any surgical incision, traumatic wound, burn, vaccination site, case of chickenpox, acne or even a minor scratch
Those are the keloid risks.
Preterm birth, female sex, Caucasian ancestry, low birth weight, a multiple gestation birth, and a placental abnormality in the pregnancy
Those are infantile hemangioma associations.
Age over forty, sun exposure, very fair skin that always burns and never tans, male sex, tattoos with red ink, skin trauma such as lasers, surgery or cryotherapy, and human papillomavirus infection

set1.q: Where is a keratoacanthoma believed to arise from, and what is its relationship to squamous cell carcinoma?
opts: The pilosebaceous unit; it is argued to be a variant of invasive squamous cell carcinoma

Correct — it is histopathologically similar to squamous cell carcinoma, and strong arguments support classifying it as a variant of the invasive form. That is why the standard of care is to excise or destroy it rather than watch it.
The eccrine sweat duct; it is histopathologically quite distinct from squamous cell carcinoma and carries no malignant potential at all
That is closer to syringoma, and it understates the concern here.
The dermal fibroblast; it is histopathologically similar to a hypertrophic scar and does not ever behave in a malignant fashion
That describes dermatofibroma.
The sebaceous gland; it is a crowding of sebocytes within an enlarged gland, with no known potential for malignant transformation
That is sebaceous hyperplasia.

That is the keratoacanthoma differential.

A benign neoplasm of eccrine ducts, appearing at puberty and more often in females
Correct — eccrine, meaning sweat gland.
A benign neoplasm of endothelial cells, appearing in the first weeks of life and more often in females
That is infantile hemangioma.
A benign nerve sheath tumour, appearing at puberty and increasing with age

Given before excision to reduce the size of the lesion; it inhibits deoxyribonucleic acid synthesis in actively dividing cells
Correct — a chemotherapeutic agent used as a surgical adjunct.
Given after excision in order to prevent recurrence; it inhibits fibroblast proliferation within the healing wound bed

Given instead of excision in frail patients; it induces microvascular thrombosis within the vessels feeding the lesion

set2.q: What is the standard of care for removing an epidermoid cyst, and what is the option for a small one?
opts: Removal of the entire capsule when the cyst is not inflamed; a small one can be punched and emptied

Correct — the capsule is the part that matters, and removing all of it is the standard of care. A cyst of one to three centimetres can instead be treated with a punch incision and removal of the contents.
Simple drainage of the keratin contents through a stab incision, leaving the capsule in place to scar down on its own
Leaving the capsule is what the standard of care avoids.
Elliptical excision with five-millimetre margins in every case, with the specimen sent for histopathological analysis
Those margins belong to keratoacanthoma.
Scissor excision at the level of the stalk followed by electrodesiccation, with no local anesthesia required
That is how skin tags are removed.

set2.q: What does sebaceous hyperplasia look like?
opts: Multiple skin-coloured papules of one to two millimetres on the eyelids and upper cheeks
That is syringoma.
A firm nodule with a brown halo and a scaly raised centre, usually on a leg
That is the dermatofibroma.
Soft whitish-yellow papules with a central umbilication, on the face
Correct — single or multiple, two to nine millimetres, and a very small globule of sebum can sometimes be expressed from the centre.
Soft yellow cholesterol plaques on the medial eyelids, without any umbilication
That is xanthelasma.

set2.q: What determines the management of a cutaneous horn?
opts: The cosmetic concern of the patient alone, since the underlying lesion is benign in essentially every case
The lesion is not always benign, which is precisely the point.
The underlying etiology, with excision to the standard for the tumour type and location if malignant
Correct — you treat what is at the base, not the horn.
The height of the horn itself, with excision reserved for any projection measuring over one centimetre
Size of the projection is not what drives the decision.
The patient's age at presentation, with watchful observation preferred in anyone over the age of seventy
Age is not the management criterion given.

set2.q: What is a telangiectasia?
opts: A congenital dilation of dermal capillaries through the full depth of the dermis, present at birth
That is nevus flammeus.
An acquired proliferation of capillaries and venules forming a deep red papule under five millimetres
That is the cherry angioma.
A rapidly growing vascular papule that arises in response to trauma or hormonal change
That is the pyogenic granuloma.
A permanently dilated capillary under one millimetre, blanchable
Correct — an acquired vascular lesion, single or in groups, with a central punctum. It may be primary or secondary and is associated with numerous diseases.

set2.q: What should a patient be told about cherry angiomas?
opts: New lesions will likely develop and there is no way to prevent them
Correct — treatment is not necessary unless they bother the patient.
They are premalignant and each one should be biopsied before removal
Cherry angiomas are benign and require no biopsy.
They indicate a lipid disorder and warrant fasting cholesterol testing
That association belongs to xanthelasma.
They will fade within a year, so no intervention is needed
Fading within a year is nevus simplex.

set2.q: How does a plexiform neurofibroma differ from a cutaneous one?
opts: It is confined to the brain and spinal cord and never involves peripheral tissue
The deck says it occurs anywhere except those two sites.
It is a pigmented macule rather than a tumour, and it grows with the child
That is the café au lait spot.
It is a tumour in the tissue covering the nerves, occurs anywhere except brain and spinal cord, and is large and extensive
Correct — and it may be locally invasive.
It is a discrete mass arising from a single peripheral nerve, sits just above or under the skin, and stays well circumscribed
That describes the cutaneous neurofibroma instead.

set2.q: What is the difference between a sinus and a fistula?
opts: A sinus follows a surgical wound; a fistula is always congenital in origin
Both usually follow an abscess rather than differing in origin this way.
A sinus is a blind track; a fistula is a track connecting two epithelium-lined surfaces
Correct — both usually arise from a preceding abscess.
A sinus connects two epithelium-lined surfaces; a fistula is a blind-ending track
This reverses the two definitions.
A sinus is lined by keratin; a fistula is lined by granulation tissue only
The distinction is about where the track ends, not what lines it.

set2.q: What do syringomas look like, and where do they sit?
opts: Light tan to brown macules over five millimetres, appearing in the first year of life
Those are café au lait spots.
Multiple skin-coloured, pink or brown papules of one to two millimetres, most often on the eyelids and upper cheeks
Correct — the periorbital location is the recognisable part.
Multiple whitish-yellow papules of two to nine millimetres with central umbilication, most often on the face
That is sebaceous hyperplasia.
Soft yellow cholesterol plaques, most often on the medial eyelids
That is xanthelasma, which shares the site but not the appearance.

set2.q: What should a keloid-prone patient be advised to avoid?
opts: Cosmetic procedures such as ear piercing, and body piercings generally
Correct — prevention is called the most important treatment.
Sun exposure during peak hours, and tanning beds at any time
That is the general benign-lesion counselling instead.
Tight footwear and walking barefoot without socks
That is corn and callus education.
Oral contraceptives and any medication affecting the liver
That history matters for spider angioma.

set2.q: What is the dimple sign, and which lesion shows it?
opts: The lesion retracts beneath the skin surface with lateral compression; dermatofibroma
Correct — this is the physical sign the lecture asks about directly.
The lesion blanches completely under direct downward pressure; cherry angioma
Blanching is a vascular finding rather than the dimple sign.
The lesion transmits a wave-like fluid shift on palpation; pilonidal abscess
That is fluctuance, which indicates a fluid-filled lesion.
The lesion expresses pasty material through a central pore; epidermoid cyst
That is the punctum and its contents, not a dimple.

set2.q: What is the defining physical finding of a keloid?
opts: It stays confined within the margins of the original wound
Staying inside the wound margins is the hypertrophic scar.
It retracts beneath the skin on lateral compression
That is the dimple sign of a dermatofibroma.
It blanches completely with direct pressure
Blanching is a vascular lesion finding rather than a scar finding.
It extends beyond the margins of the original wound
Correct — that single feature separates it from a hypertrophic scar.

set2.q: What should be screened for in a patient with xanthelasma, and why does it matter?
opts: Liver disease; it may signify increased risk of variceal bleeding
Liver disease is the association drawn for spider angioma instead.
Hyperlipidemia; it may signify increased risk of cardiac disease
Correct — the lesion is associated with lipid disorders.
Diabetes mellitus; it may signify increased risk of peripheral neuropathy
The named association is with lipid disorders rather than glucose.
Thyroid dysfunction; it may signify increased risk of periorbital myxoedema
No thyroid association is described for this lesion.

set2.q: Which site of intertriginous freckling is NOT listed as a diagnostic criterion?
opts: The inguinal region
The inguinal region is the other named diagnostic site.
Both the axilla and the inguinal region
Both of these are the listed diagnostic sites.
Under the breasts
Correct — it may be observed there, but the criteria name axilla and groin.
The axilla
The axillary region is one of the two named diagnostic sites.

set2.q: What is xanthelasma made of, and where does it sit?
opts: A collection of mucin extruded from a joint space, most commonly over a distal finger joint
That is the digital mucous cyst.
A crowding of sebocytes within an enlarged gland, most commonly on the face
That is sebaceous hyperplasia.
A collection of lipid-laden macrophages forming soft yellow cholesterol plaques, most commonly on the medial eyelids
Correct — and it is asymptomatic.
A collection of keratin within an enclosed epithelial sac, most commonly on the face, scalp and trunk
That is the epidermoid cyst.

set2.q: Where do calluses typically develop, and what happens if the process is acute and severe?
opts: On the palms of the hands or the balls of the feet; a blister forms
Correct — a blister is the acute end of the same friction process.
In the fourth-to-fifth toe web space, where the skin macerates; an abscess forms
That web space is the soft corn's site, and abscess is not the sequel.
On the dorsal and lateral fifth toe, over the joint; a deep ulcer forms
That is the hard corn's site, and ulceration is not what is described.
Over the sacrum and other bony prominences; a black eschar forms
Those are pressure injury sites rather than callus sites.

set2.q: In what circumstance do hypertrophic scars characteristically occur?
opts: When a wound is left to heal by secondary intention rather than closed
Method of closure is not what the table names.
When the patient has dark skin, which is strongly associated with them
Dark skin colour is associated with keloids; hypertrophic scars have no such association.
When a wound becomes infected during the proliferative phase of healing
Infection is not the circumstance given.
When scars cross joints or skin creases at a right angle
Correct — and they develop soon after surgery rather than months later.

set2.q: What is the differential diagnosis for a pyogenic granuloma?
opts: Keloid, hypertrophic scar and foreign-body granuloma, the fibrous group
Those are the abnormal wound healing differentials.
Cherry angioma, malignant melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma
Correct — two malignancies, which is why treatment is often taken up.
Nevus flammeus and infantile hemangioma, the two congenital vascular lesions
Those form the hemangioma differential rather than this one.
Milia, xanthelasma and basal cell carcinoma, the periorbital group
That is the syringoma differential.

set2.q: When do café au lait spots appear, and how do they change?
opts: Usually after the age of fifty, on sun-exposed skin; they darken with further exposure
That is the solar lentigo from Lecture 3.
Usually in the first weeks of life; they proliferate and then involute
That is the infantile hemangioma.
Usually at birth or in the first year; they grow in proportion to the child
Correct — often the first manifestation of neurofibromatosis type 1.
Usually at puberty; they increase in number and size with age
That is the cutaneous neurofibroma's timing.

set2.q: What should the history cover in a patient with spider angiomas?
opts: Pregnancies, hormone use, alcohol history, and medications that carry a risk of liver damage
Correct — the lesion can be a marker of estrogen excess or liver disease.
Birth history, feeding and weight gain, and any family history of vascular birthmarks
That is the infantile hemangioma history.
Footwear, occupation and use of tools or sports equipment
That is the corn and callus history.
Immobility, incontinence and nutritional status
Those are the pressure injury questions.

set2.q: When is a lipoma treated?
opts: When cosmetically deforming, or the diagnosis is uncertain
Correct — an enlarged deforming mass or diagnostic uncertainty can be treated surgically with excision. Asymptomatic tumours can simply be observed.
Always at diagnosis, because of the risk of transformation to liposarcoma
No such transformation risk is described here.
Only once it exceeds ten centimetres, regardless of symptoms or appearance
No size threshold is given for treatment.
Only after a trial of intralesional corticosteroid has failed to shrink it
Steroid injection is not offered for lipoma.

set2.q: What is the differential diagnosis for a dermatofibroma?
opts: Squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, amelanotic melanoma and molluscum contagiosum
That is the keratoacanthoma differential.
Cystic acne, lipoma, neurofibroma, keratoacanthoma and basal cell carcinoma
That is the epidermoid cyst differential.
Milia, xanthelasma and basal cell carcinoma, all of which sit around the eye
That is the syringoma differential.
Basal cell carcinoma, hypertrophic scar, cutaneous melanoma and keratoacanthoma
Correct — two of the four are malignancies, which is why it matters.

set2.q: What is the natural history of a hypertrophic scar?
opts: It enlarges continuously for months to years and does not regress
That is the keloid's course.
It grows rapidly for six to eight weeks and then involutes over three to six months
That triphasic course is the keratoacanthoma's.
It is present at birth, grows with the child, and never involutes
That is nevus flammeus.
It remains stable and then regresses, flattening with time
Correct — which is why observation is reasonable.

set2.q: What causes a pressure injury?
opts: Disruption of the skin over the coccyx drawing in hair and debris, with follicular plugging that prevents drainage
That is the pilonidal cyst.
Loss of the control mechanisms that normally regulate tissue repair, producing overgrowth of dense fibrous tissue
That is abnormal wound healing, giving keloid or hypertrophic scar.
Unrelieved pressure damaging underlying tissue, generally soft tissue compressed between a bony prominence and an external surface for a prolonged time
Correct — the injury ranges from intact skin to ulcers reaching bone.
Repeated friction over a broad area of skin, producing diffuse hyperkeratosis with a poorly defined margin and no central keratin core at all
That is the callus.

set2.q: What is an acrochordon, anatomically?
opts: A cystic enclosure of epithelium within the dermis, filled with keratin
That is an epidermoid cyst.
A localised overgrowth of fat cells within the subcutaneous tissue
That is a lipoma.
A fibroepithelial pedunculated papilloma, with a narrow stalk and a broad tip
Correct — which is why it can be snipped off at the stalk.
A benign neoplasm of eccrine ducts, appearing in crops around the eyes
That is a syringoma.

set2.q: Where does a digital mucous cyst sit, and what can it do to the nail?
opts: Over the distal interphalangeal joint; it may groove the nail
Correct — a translucent skin-coloured papule on the distal aspect of the digit, over the proximal nail matrix or the nail bed. Pressure on the matrix causes a longitudinal groove.
Over the proximal interphalangeal joint; pressure on the nail bed may cause pitting
The joint named is the distal interphalangeal, and the change is a groove.
Along the lateral nail fold; it causes retraction of the cuticle over months
That is chronic paronychia from Lecture 4.
Under the free edge of the nail; it causes complete separation of the nail plate
Onycholysis is not what this lesion produces.

set2.q: What is the earliest sign of an infantile hemangioma?
opts: A flat well-circumscribed blanchable patch that darkens with crying, fever or overheating
That is nevus flammeus.
A pink to erythematous irregular macule that becomes more noticeable when the baby cries
That is nevus simplex, the stork bite.
A bright red exophytic papule with a moist surface that bleeds after minor trauma
That is pyogenic granuloma.
Blanching of the involved skin, then fine telangiectasias, then a red or crimson macule
Correct — about half are present at birth as a prominent cutaneous mark.

set2.q: What must a patient be told before electing cosmetic removal of a benign lesion?
opts: The likelihood that the lesion will become malignant if left
These are benign lesions, so this would be untrue.
The risk of pigmentary changes and the chance of recurrence
Correct — both must be fully explained beforehand.
The need for lifelong surveillance of the site afterwards
Lifelong surveillance is not what the slide requires.
The requirement for histopathological analysis in every case
Histology is not mandated for every cosmetic removal.

set2.q: How are corns and calluses managed?
opts: Intralesional corticosteroid injection, with silicone gel sheeting worn daily
Those are keloid and hypertrophic scar treatments.
Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen, repeated at two-week intervals until resolved
Cryotherapy is used for other lesions here, not as the first move for corns.
Elliptical surgical excision with five-millimetre margins, sent for histology
That is keratoacanthoma's management, where malignancy is the concern.
Padding and avoiding poorly fitting footwear, with over-the-counter keratolytic products
Correct — remove the pressure first, then thin the keratin.
